newsitem.title: USA: Heavy placements keep U.S. fed cattle numbers high.
newsitem.headline: Heavy placements keep U.S. fed cattle numbers high.

text.p: The number of cattle in large U.S. feedlots as of April 1 was above a year earlier with placements during March again exceeding the year-earlier level and offsetting active marketings, livestock analysts said.
The U.S. Agriculture Department is expected to confirm the large fed cattle supply on Friday in its monthly Cattle on Feed report, set for release at 1400 CDT (1900 GMT).

Analysts projected the data will show the number of cattle on feed in feedlots of 1,000 head or more capacity in the seven key states on April 1 at an average 107.6 percent of a year ago. Estimates ranged from 106.0 to 108.7 percent.

They said placement data will again be the most important part of the report. March seven-state placement estimates again ranged widely, averaging 103.3 percent of a year ago in a Reuter pre-report survey, and ranging from 100.5 to 107.0 percent.
Profit margins for feedlots remained fairly positive in March and feed costs were not considered burdensome which drew cattle into feedyards, sources said.
"They (feeders) were making money and corn was at a good price -- way cheaper than a year ago," said Joe Kropf of Kropf and Love Consulting, who estimated placements at 105 percent.

Analysts continued to estimate seven-state numbers while building historical data on the new 12-state part of the report. USDA made revisions to its seven-state report and introduced a 12-state report in January 1996.
The March cattle marketings estimates ranged widely this time and may be of more importance than recent reports, they said.
Marketing estimates averaged 100.6 percent of a year ago, and ranged from 98.0 to 104.5 percent.

"Trade is fearful of a low $60 market and that keeps feedlots marketing on a timely basis," said David Holloway, market analyst for Koch Beef Company, who closely watches the reports for Koch's feedlot business.
Cash cattle sold in brisk activity Tuesday at central and southern Plains feedlots mostly at $69.00 per cwt, with a few pens of exceptional quality animals in Texas bringing $70.00.

Holloway said he thought the USDA's March marketings figure may be of increased importance because the market is at a turning point. Fed cattle numbers should rise as the summer progresses, which typically also is the strongest time of year for beef demand.
The report's marketings figure should show an active pace which would indicate currentness.

"We have been marketing cattle aggressively as an industry and now that we have seen that slow down a bit, the marketings number will take on more importance as we head into the (larger) summer" supplies, Holloway said.
"Marketings anywhere around unchanged is a good number -- that would have kept the lots current," Kropf added.
